learningObjective: Identify the defining properties of a dataflow / computational graph as used by deep learning compilers.

canonicalClaims.claim: A deep-learning computational graph is a directed graph where nodes represent operations and edges represent tensor values flowing from a producer to one or more consumers; the graph is typically a DAG within a single forward pass and each edge carries an inferred shape and dtype.
conditions: The graph represents a feedforward computation.
The framework supports shape/type inference for its ops.
nonImplications: Does not imply every workload produces a DAG (control flow can require additional constructs).
Does not imply shape inference always yields fully static shapes.

misconceptions.claim: Every edge in the graph must be materialized in memory as an intermediate tensor.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Materialization is a codegen/scheduling decision; fused kernels avoid it.

misconceptions.claim: The graph is a general directed graph with cycles by default.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Forward passes typically form DAGs; explicit constructs are used for loops.

misconceptions.claim: Nodes represent tensor values and edges represent operations.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The mapping is the opposite in standard dataflow graphs.

misconceptions.claim: Shape inference is optional and cannot fail gracefully.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Frameworks provide shape inference as a routine analysis; failures produce diagnostics or dynamic shapes.

implementationFacts: PyTorch FX graph, TVM Relax, XLA HLO all use directed dataflow representations
Static shape/dtype inference is a routine graph analysis; dynamic dims may remain symbolic
Fused kernels do not require additional graph nodes
performanceScenarios: Graph-level analyses (fusion, layout, constant folding) exploit DAG structure and shape/dtype annotations.
